title: Investigating the role of GATAD2 and the NuRD complex in FOXO/daf-16 regulation of stem cell fate
text:
This proposal addresses how developmental pathways are regulated so that stem cells can produce
all of the types of cells that are needed for a tissue to develop and remain healthy over time . This
work will decipher a new regulatory pathway involving three evolutionarily conserved components:
the FOXO transcription factor, three RNA-binding proteins, and GATAD2A/B, using the tractable C.
elegans model system. Unraveling the genetic and molecular details by which these proteins interact
to regulate cell fate during quiescence will illuminate fundamental stem cell biology, laying the
foundation for future clinical applications.

title: Data Coordinating Center for Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet
text: This application is for the continuation of the Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet Coordinating Center at the University of South Florida. The goal of Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet is the prevention of type 1 diabetes in individuals at-risk for its development. Identification of individuals at elevated risk of developing the disease will provide more information about risk factors, leading to a better understanding of disease pathogenesis.

title: Novel approaches to identify tandem repeat expansions in neurodegenerative disease
text:
The set of genes that cause Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are still far from clear. We have established a novel
pipeline to quantify the contribution of tandem repeats throughout the human genome and have identified
several repeats with AD-specific repeat expansions. We propose to interrogate the contribution of these
repeats to disease pathogenesis and their mechanism of action.

title: University of Rochester Clinical Site within the NEXT Network of Clinical Trials
text: Rigorous clinical trials are essential for the translation of scientific discoveries to improve the health of children and adults with neurological disease. The University of Rochester and its neuroscience investigators have the clinical trials experience, expertise, and track record to serve as an exemplary and high-quality Clinical Site to ensure the success of NeuroNEXT.

title: Large-scale Disease Pathway Discovery by Integrating Tissue-specific Molecular Networks via Hierarchical Bayesian Inference on Graph Neural Networks
text:
Advancing our knowledge of molecular interaction networks is a fundamental goal in Systems Biology. Our proposed research program will create transformative bio-statistical graph representation learning strategies and
bio-medical data analytics to elucidate a holistic view of large-scale disease pathways. A quantitative and mechanistic understanding of molecular interactions that construct pathways leading to distinct disease phenotypes
will accelerate the development of new therapies to combat many human diseases like cancer, cardiovascular
disease, neurodegenerative conditions, and metabolic diseases.

title: Directing and Deciphering Macrophage Polarization through Biologically-Inspired Surface Design of Polymer Brush-Coated Cell Culture Substrates
text:
We will engineer polymer brush grafted cell culture substrates that fill critical knowledge gaps in macrophage
(Mp) biology by recapitulating spatially complex patterns of ligand presentation during Mp polarization. In the first
three projects, we will functionalize polymer brushes with one of three ligands (differentially sulfated glycosa-
minoglycan mimics, phosphatidyl serine, or mannose), culture Mps on substrates grafted with ligand-functional-
ized polymer brushes, and interrogate Mp phenotype as a function of ligand spatial presentation. In the fourth
project, we will graft ligand-functionalized polymer brushes from multi-compartmental electrospun scaffolds, pro-
gram desired combinations of mechanical, topographical and biochemical cues, and clarify how the interplay
between physical and chemical dimensions of the culture environment sculpts Mp polarization.

title: Epigenetic Regulation of Trained Immunity in Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms and Dissections
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms and
dissections are frequent causes of death in the United States, largely because current medications are
ineffective. The project is relevant to the NHLBI’s mission because it focuses on the treatment and prevention
of life-threating cardiovascular disease; the development of new, effective medications would prevent the
progression of aortic disease and save the lives of patients with these conditions.

title: PDGF-BB and the metastatic brain microenvironment
text:
Women diagnosed with breast cancer-associated brain metastases (BCBM) have an unacceptable median
overall survival rate of 10-11 months. A major knowledge gap in understanding brain metastasis biology is the
functional interplay between tumor cells and the metastatic brain tumor microenvironment (TME). The current
application will advance this field by directly examining novel mechanisms of how the PDGFB–to-PDGFRβ
signaling node, which is potentially druggable, promotes BCBM by creating a pro-tumorigenic immune
microenvironment and by invoking vascular changes in collaboration with Angiopoietin-1.

title: Biostatistics/Epidemiology Training Grants in AIDS
text:
The Biostatistics and Epidemiology in AIDS Training Program at the Harvard T. H. Chan School of
Public Health prepares predoctoral and postdoctoral trainees in the application of biostatistics and
epidemiology to HIV/AIDS research. The Program combines first class training in the development of
theory and methods in the fields of biostatistics, epidemiology, computational biology/bioinformatics
and health data science relevant to HIV research, with practical experience in HIV research
collaborations in multidisciplinary team science settings. The Program also provides trainees with the
skills necessary for scientific leadership in interdisciplinary settings, focusing on skills for
collaboration, communication, grant writing and career development.

title: Effects of TBI on the Neuronal Assemblies and Coupled Oscillations Underlying Cognition
text:
Although cognitive dysfunction is often a debilitating and persistent symptom of traumatic brain injury (TBI), there
are currently no effective treatments available. This project will define for the first time the underlying functional
basis for cognitive dysfunction in biomechanically relevant TBI models using advanced electrophysiology
measures and behavioral tasks. These experiments will lead to crucial mechanisms that can be translated in
the future to clinical treatments for cognitive dysfunction post-TBI.

title: Targeting microbial triggers of gammopathy for immunoprevention
text:
These studies target the precursor state to multiple myeloma, called monoclonal gammopathy
of undetermined significance. It will test how specific bacteria can be involved in promoting the
growth of tumor cells and dissect the mechanisms underlying inflammation induced by such
bacteria. Targeting these triggers may lead to novel approaches for immune prevention of
myeloma and improve outcome of these patients.

title: Altered central carbon metabolism in mitochondrial myopathy
text:
Mitochondrial dysfunction affects approximately 1 in 5000 individuals, resulting in diseases with limited to no
treatment options. Targeting metabolic pathways offers an attractive route to engineer novel therapies;
however, a detailed knowledge of metabolism in the disease state is missing. By characterizing metabolic
fluxes in animals and humans with mitochondrial disease, we will identify therapeutic pathways which may be
targeted to benefit patients.

title: Multi-Omics Core C
text:
MULTI-OMICS CORE C NARRATIVE
Early life stress is a significant and understudied risk factor for increasing cardiovascular disease risk later in life.
Core C will prepare samples and coordinate multiple genome wide analyses (multi-omics) from the level of a
single nucleus to the tissue for all the Projects in this grant application. Centralizing the multi-omic approaches
in Core C will ensure rigor and reproducibility of experimental design and data collection to meet the goals of
this highly functioning PPG.

title: Understanding melanocyte-keratinocyte interactions in normal and malignant states
text:
Basal cell carcinoma is the most common keratinocyte-derived malignancy with similarities to a dysregulated
hair follicle. The role of melanocytes in this cancer is poorly understood, but preliminary data suggests a potential
pathogenic role. The goal is to understand the crosstalk that occurs between keratinocytes and melanocytes in
normal and malignant contexts and thus develop Dr. Pedersen’s training as a physician scientist.

title: North Carolina Agricultural and Technincal State University: Research Centers in Minority Institutions (RCMI)
text:
OVERALL CORE PROJECT NARRATIVE
The North Carolina A&T State University RCMI proposed program focuses on brain health and associated
cardiometabolic disease health disparities. The RCMI will support two R01-scale research projects and a pilot
project program to identify cardiometabolic biomarkers, develop cost effective nanosenors and bioelectronic
devices for early detection, risk assessment, and evaluation of therapeutic outcomes while implementing
culturally relevant interventions to promote brain health. This proposal is relevant to NIH’s mission of enhancing
and improving health and reducing illness and disability by fostering fundamental creative and innovative
discoveries.

title: ARCH REACH Implementation and Biostatistics Methods Core
text: HIV and unhealthy alcohol use (UAU) disproportionately impact marginalized groups, including those minoritized secondary to race, ethnicity, sex, gender identity, and sexual orientation and those of lower socioeconomic status. ARCH-REACH extends prior work of the ARCH Research Consortium in the CNICS Cohorts to address alcohol-related inequities among PWH. A fundamental goal of this research is to expand the knowledge base regarding the relationship between alcohol use and clinically relevant health outcomes through the lens of important social determinants. This is especially critical because 1) alcohol exposures – including fundamental causes like social and structural determinants of health – are often inadequately measured, 2) alcohol reduction interventions are often inequitably implemented, and 3), changing definitions of recovery from unhealthy alcohol use may further widen health disparities if not evaluated from a structural determinism lens. Therefore, the overarching goal of the ARCH-REACH Implementation Science and Biostatistics Methods Core (ARCH-MC) is to ensure that high quality research is performed by all program components using advanced statistical approaches and implementation science methodology specifically aimed at understanding and reducing the fundamental causes of alcohol-related disparities for PWH. Under Dr. Joseph Delaney’s direction, ARCH-MC will apply cutting edge machine learning and causal inference methods that properly incorporate considerations of intersectionality and further characterize social and structural determinants that predict and explain patterns of co-morbid alcohol use and worsening HIV. Under Dr. Emily Williams’ direction, ARCH-MC will conduct rigorous formative evaluation of the two implementation projects to assess implementation determinants that contribute to inequitable delivery of evidence-based alcohol reduction interventions for PWH. ARCH-MC will also provide continuous methodological support on all ARCH-REACH components via content expertise, coordination, and alignment of analytic approaches across projects, sharable resources, and bi-directional feedback with the community advisory board (Dissemination Core). These resources will augment learnings across ARCH-REACH projects and directly advance ARCH-REACH goals for understanding and reducing health disparities among PWH.

title: Core C - Modeling Core
text: SARS-CoV-2 infection leads to different clinical outcomes that range from mild symptoms to hospitalization and sometimes death. However, biomarkers predictive of COVID-10 disease outcomes (i.e., symptoms severity, viral replication), which are key for preventive medicine, have not yet been identified. Importantly, elucidation of the molecular components that govern predictive signatures of clinical outcomes will provide important clues that will guide the development of novel therapeutic strategies. This U19 will build on a wealth of data gathered by the previous FluOMICS next-generation scientist and pursue two converging hypotheses 1) host innate immune response pathways triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection determine the pathogenic outcome of COVID-19 disease 2) the crosstalk between SARS-CoV-2 variants and these host innate pathways results in different transcriptional and post-translational signatures contributing to the difference in disease severity and host-tropism of the viruses. The primary objective of the Modeling Core will be to use network-based modeling approaches to integrate the experimental data generated by Project 1 and Project 2, identify innate biological processes that can predict COVID-19 disease outcomes and validate them functionally in collaboration with Project 1 and Project 2. In Aim 1, the Modeling Core will integrate OMIC datasets generated in Project 1 from data from Human in vivo and mice in vivo studies and processed and analyzed by the Technology Core and the Data Management and Bioinformatics Core. The Modeling core will build host response network models that depict the viral-host interaction at play in early events of COVID-19 infection and disease, i.e., viral replication, escape from the host innate immune response in natural infection and upon vaccination and triggering of the deleterious pro-inflammatory immune response. In Aim 2, the Modeling Core will apply heuristic approaches and an iterative process with Project 1 and Project 2. This approach will help identify novel pathways downstream of host-pathogen interactions. Importantly, it will guide the implementation of gene editing of these genes and pathways in Project 2 to validate these models and improve their accuracy experimentally; It will help understand how SARS- CoV-2 variants affect the viral-host networks built-in Aim 1. In Aim 3, the Modeling Core will use experimentally identified 3D structures of viral-host interactions and an artificial intelligence model, AlphaFold, to identify virus-host interaction in the bat, the natural host of the coronaviruses, and compare them to interactions in humans to study host-tropism of the virus and infer how these changes could impact on the pathogenic outcome of the infection. Altogether the Modeling core will provide a platform that will guide the identification and experimental validation of novel druggable targets that can stop the spread of the virus in infected hosts and worldwide populations.

title: Boston Children's Hospital/HMS Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities Research Center
text:
The goals of the Intellectual and Disabilities Research Center at Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard
Medical School are threefold: support outstanding, trans-disciplinary research into the causes of
neurodevelopmental disorders, train a diverse next generation of researchers in this field and most importantly
develop new therapies for individuals and families affected with these disorders. The Center is composed of
four scientific core facilities, each focused on a different level of investigation and complementing each other,
ranging from genetics, cellular imaging, animal behavior and physiology to clinical trials.

title: Exploring mechanisms of activation of an innate immune pathway by fungal extracellular vesicles
text:
This proposal seeks to identify the mechanism by which a human fungal pathogen, like Candida
albicans, activates the cGAS-STING pathway. Our preliminary work has identified Ca DNA
packaged in extracellular vesicles (EVs) as the fungal ligand that triggers this pathway causing a
lethal inflammatory response that clears the fungal infection. This work proposed in this project
will uncover the functional consequence of this type I IFN activation by fungal pathogens,
elucidate the activation and regulation of this signaling, and uncover a new role for diverse fungal
EVs in host cell reprogramming.

title: A non-invasive blood test for multi-cancer detection and determination of tissue of origin preceding overt cancer diagnosis
text:
Cancer is a major health burden in the United States and more sensitive screening tests are needed for early
detection. We will characterize 5-hydroxymethycytsoine (5hmC) signatures in plasma-derived cell-free DNA
(cfDNA) from PLCO subjects who were later diagnosed with common cancers. Successful completion of this
study will not only enhance our understanding of early epigenetic signs of indivudal cancer types, but also lay
the foundation for developing a non-invasive tool that improves multi-cancer early detection.
